video_title: From Chicago Pit Trader to Robinhood Exec · Steve Quirk
gist: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood and a Chicago options market maker since 1987, traces the path from the open-outcry pits through thinkorswim and TD Ameritrade to Robinhood, arguing the retail playing field has been leveled beyond anything imaginable in the late 1980s. The investor-relevant substance sits in the operating disclosures he volunteers (27.5 million customers with half new to markets, average age 36, roughly 98% of options trades on mobile, IPO allocations rising from 1-2% to 20%, average PDT-flagged account of $13,000, cash sweep at 3-3.5%) and in three structural theses: retail participation growth is a secular acceleration rather than a COVID-era blip, international penetration in the teens versus 60% of US households is the next leg, and access barriers like the PDT rule and accreditation standards are falling.

insights.claim: Steve Quirk argues the defining psychological edge of professional trading is accepting a roughly 50% wrong rate as normal, with 51% correct being enough to win, a wiring he says almost no other business tolerates.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: A base-rate framing worth importing into portfolio review: judge process and expectancy rather than hit rate, and size so that a 50% loss rate is survivable.
insights.quote: there's an expectation that you're going to be wrong about 50% of the time and you're good with it

insights.claim: Quirk's market-making risk routine was to price the absolute worst-case outcome of a trade first and then work upward to the best case, so that the downside scenario, when it arrives, produces no emotional reaction.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: A pre-mortem discipline that converts drawdowns from surprises into priced-in events; the practical test of any position is whether its worst case was written down before entry.
insights.quote: we look at the absolute worst case scenario of that trade and then work our way up to what's the best case scenario

insights.claim: Quirk attributes panic selling primarily to investors never having quantified their maximum downside, and secondarily to positions that are simply sized too large.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Two diagnosable failure modes: if a strategy or client cannot state a maximum loss, forced-liquidation risk is understated no matter how good the thesis.
insights.quote: The people that panicked the most with investments or trades are the ones that don't understand what the what the largest downside is because when when it hits they they just freak out.

insights.claim: Quirk identifies myopic fixation on one losing trade as the fastest way traders fail, arguing the ability to abandon a position and move on is a survival prerequisite because not every trade can be repaired.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Screen traders and strategies for willingness to take the loss and reset; inability to detach is a leading indicator of blow-up risk.
insights.quote: You can't In other words, you can't always fix something. You got to just flick it and move on.

insights.claim: Across the 1987 crash, dot-com, the financial crisis, COVID and the meme era, Quirk's common thread is that crises are triggered by previously unknown mechanisms rather than the risks everyone already fears, citing credit default swaps before 2007-08 as the example.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Implies consensus tail hedges are usually aimed at the wrong catalyst; the productive work is inventorying instruments and plumbing nobody has stress-tested.
insights.quote: it's not the known that causes these, it's the unknown

insights.claim: Before October 1987 there was effectively no options skew, with a 10% out-of-the-money put and a 10% out-of-the-money call priced evenly, a convention the crash permanently destroyed.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Concrete reminder that persistent put skew is a learned artifact of a single event rather than a law of nature, and that regime breaks can reprice whole option surfaces for decades.
insights.quote: the market, you know, walks up the steps and falls out the window

insights.claim: After the 1987 crash exchanges shortened trading hours to roughly 9:30 to 1:30 because there was no clarity on which clearing and trading firms would survive, and circuit-breaker halts did not yet exist.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Historical precedent for session-shortening as a crisis tool, and a reminder that clearing solvency rather than price is usually the binding constraint in a dislocation.

insights.claim: Quirk cites a VIX in the sub-16 to 18 range despite the current list of negative catalysts and elevated energy prices as the market development that most recently overturned his expectations, concluding that markets are never fully figured out.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: A veteran options practitioner flagging compressed volatility as inconsistent with the macro backdrop, which is the setup where cheap convexity is worth revisiting.
insights.quote: I've learned to never say never.

themes.theme: Collapse of the Cost and Data Moat

insights.claim: Quirk's floor-trading firm paid roughly $10,000 a month for a brick-sized handheld providing quotes and order entry, functionality he says is inferior to what any retail user now gets free on an iPhone.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: A hard benchmark for how completely the market-data and execution moat eroded; the surviving edge in brokerage is distribution and design, not tooling.
insights.quote: it cost us 10 grand a month. 10 grand a month we paid for that technology

insights.claim: In the late 1980s retail investors paid $75 to $80 per trade while floor professionals paid essentially nothing, and also lacked the information access and education professionals had, a three-part gap Quirk says has since been closed.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Quantifies the commission compression that underwrote the retail participation boom, leaving product access rather than price as the remaining differentiator between platforms.

insights.claim: European exchange demutualization opened market making to any participant and drove a build-out of broad electronic access technology roughly seven to eight years before the equivalent shift reached the US, an edge Quirk carried into retail platform building.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: A template for how venue ownership structure gates technology adoption; member-owned venues elsewhere are candidates for the same repricing of access.
insights.quote: as soon as they went public, now the whole world is a market maker. Anybody can be a market maker.

insights.claim: Robinhood has roughly 27.5 million customers of whom about half are new to the market, a mix Quirk frames as creating an affirmative financial-literacy and suitability obligation for the firm.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Half the base being first-time investors is simultaneously the growth story and the regulatory exposure; education spend should be modeled as compliance cost, not marketing.
insights.quote: half of our 27 and a half million customers are new to the market

insights.claim: Quirk says Robinhood is the largest retail options trading firm and until recently executed about 98% of its options trades on a phone, a share now closer to 95% as the desktop Legend platform grows.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Mobile-native options flow at this scale is a distinctive order-flow profile, and the Legend-driven drift toward desktop signals a deliberate move upmarket into more active traders.
insights.quote: the largest option retail option trading firm, which is Robinhood today, is doing 98% of their trades on a phone

insights.claim: Quirk pushes back on the perception that Robinhood is dominated by all-day active traders, saying the lion's share of customers are buy-and-hold investors who put only a small slice of the portfolio into whatever theme is hot, such as AI or energy story stocks.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: If accurate, the revenue base is less cyclical than a pure day-trading proxy implies, and Robinhood flow reads as a barometer of retail thematic allocation rather than churn.
insights.quote: Most of them, you know, are people that are buy and hold.

insights.claim: Robinhood's average customer age is 36 versus roughly 60 at TD Ameritrade and Schwab, a gap Quirk says forces contextual on-demand education embedded in the product pathway instead of the long-form in-person seminars that once drew 600 to 700 people per room.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: A roughly 24-year age gap between platforms implies decades of asset-transfer tailwind for the younger franchise and structurally different servicing economics at each.
insights.quote: average age is 60, and they they learn in a different way than, you know, the people that are in their 30s

insights.claim: Quirk cites Robinhood cash sweep paying around 3 to 3.5%, which he tells nervous investors is roughly 20 times a bank deposit rate, positioning it as the release valve for volatility discomfort rather than selling out.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Cash sweep doubles as a retention product that keeps de-risking clients on-platform instead of transferring to banks, a meaningful net-interest and stickiness lever.
insights.quote: That is 20 times what you're getting at your bank.

insights.claim: Quirk argues the retail participation surge during the stimulus-check and meme-stock era was an acceleration of a long-running secular trend rather than a blip, noting retail's share has kept rising across equities, options, crypto and futures.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: The core structural bet behind retail brokerage valuations; if the trend is secular, drawdowns in retail volumes are cyclical entry points rather than trend breaks.
insights.quote: I just thought it was an acceleration of what was already happening

insights.claim: Quirk says the pattern day trader rule is being eliminated as of this episode's airing, following a multi-year campaign by brokerage firms, exchanges and other market participants that began before his time at Robinhood.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Removing the day-trade flag expands the addressable active-trading base at every retail broker, and the effect should surface first in small-account turnover.

insights.claim: The average Robinhood account affected by the PDT rule is about $13,000, meaning the restriction disproportionately constrained the platform's youngest and smallest customers.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Sizes the affected cohort directly: repeal is a volume unlock concentrated in small accounts, the segment most inclined toward options and leveraged products.

insights.claim: Quirk argues PDT was a defensible dot-com-era rule that became obsolete once clearing-firm and broker risk systems caught up 10 to 15 years ago, and that its main effects since have been pushing traders to hold losers to avoid a flag and to transfer accounts to a different broker once flagged.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Names PDT-driven account churn as a real customer-acquisition cost across retail brokers, so repeal should improve retention economics industry-wide.
insights.quote: as soon as they hit their flag, they just transfer out of Robinhood and go open an account at the broker XYZ and start over

insights.claim: Quirk says he used to teach traders to move into futures specifically to escape PDT, preferring the ES future over SPY because futures carry no day-trade count and no short-sale constraints.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Part of retail futures volume was regulatory arbitrage rather than product preference, so PDT repeal could pull some of that flow back into cash equities and ETFs.
insights.quote: Trade futures. They don't have these stupid rules.

insights.claim: Robinhood's IPO Access allocations have shifted from the firm scratching and clawing for 1% to 2% of a deal to issuers proactively offering 20%, which Quirk calls the most positive development for retail customers.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: A roughly tenfold shift in retail allocation power changes IPO book-building dynamics and gives retail platforms a genuine issuer-side product to monetize.
insights.quote: we used to scratch and claw to get 1% or 2%. Now, we're having firms come to us and say we want to give you 20%.

insights.claim: Quirk attacks accreditation rules as illogical, contrasting a 54-year-old deemed qualified because of a $10 million inheritance against a 31-year-old NASA space engineer who is not, and signals more access barriers are targeted next.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Flags the accredited-investor definition as the next regulatory wall retail platforms will push on, with private-market and pre-IPO access as the prize.
insights.quote: suddenly I'm more qualified to to to make an investment uh than a 31-year-old NASA space engineer? I don't think so

insights.claim: Quirk lists around-the-clock trading, pre-IPO securities and institutional-style IPO allocation as the specific customer demands driving Robinhood's roadmap, describing customers as pushing the firm for more once each existing capability ships.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: A stated pipeline of the next products to expect from retail brokers, each a potential fee pool and a competitive gap for incumbents that lack them.

insights.claim: Retail investing participation sits in the teens as a share in both Europe and Asia versus roughly 60% of US households, the headroom Quirk identifies as the reason Robinhood is no longer focused only on the US.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Quantifies the international opportunity that carries the growth case now that US household penetration is high and domestic account growth is a saturation story.
insights.quote: as great as the retail participation is in the US, 60% of US households, it's in the teens in Europe, it's in the teens in Asia

insights.claim: Quirk estimates 75 to 80% of what international customers want is US equities Robinhood already offers, with local work confined to country-specific wrappers such as UK ISAs and SIPPs plus FX conversion, and says foreign regulators welcome the entry because household investment wealth reduces reliance on state retirement support.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Implies unusually low marginal cost and low regulatory friction for international launches, since the product core ships unchanged and pension-burden politics works in the entrant's favor.

insights.claim: Quirk describes Asian and particularly Chinese investors as running a 'barbell economy' mindset, risking a larger share of assets in markets than US or European investors because rapid wage growth backstops them, while financial literacy there lags the US.
insights.speaker: Steve Quirk, Chief Brokerage Officer at Robinhood
insights.so_what: Higher risk budgets combined with lower literacy means Asian expansion carries both higher revenue per account and higher suitability and conduct risk.
insights.quote: They're they're more prone to take risk.
